title: Spatial and historical drivers of fake news diffusion: Evidence from anti-Muslim discrimination in India
screen_reason: The paper's aim is causal (difference-in-difference on the geographic and historical determinants of fake-news diffusion), which on its own would be excluded. But it reports a descriptive quantitative share with a denominator: the share of all georeferenced tweets posted in India that contained anti-Muslim COVID fake news, given as a daily time series with named values (about 0.1% pre-shock, 2.8% on 31 March 2020, peaking at 3.3% on 1 April 2020). Under the rule that a study whose aim is something else is still included if a descriptive share is reported anywhere, this is eligible as a CONTENT estimate.

estimates.date: 1 April 2020 (peak day of a series running 1 December 2019 to 30 April 2020; main analysis window 24 March to 6 April 2020)
estimates.measure_type: % of all georeferenced tweets posted in India in a day that contained anti-Muslim COVID-19 fake news keywords (peak day)
estimates.value_raw: the share of tweets reporting anti-Muslim false stories - around 0.1% of total tweets in the week preceding the Tablighi shock - jumped to 2.8% on March 31, then peaked at 3.3% a day later
estimates.denominator: All georeferenced tweets published in India on that day (the full 1 December 2019 - 30 April 2020 pull returned 16,967,380 tweets; the 24 March - 6 April 2020 analysis window comprises 1,863,349 tweets by 187,787 distinct users in 21,977 locations)
estimates.definition: A tweet counts if it contains at least one hashtag or keyword from a list of anti-Muslim fake-news terms compiled from false stories fact-checked by AltNews in March-April 2020 (Muslims deliberately spreading the virus by sneezing, spitting, licking or peeing; 'Corona Jihad'/'Islamic Jihadi' terms), expanded by snowballing and translated into 11 Indian languages
estimates.misinfo_def: "In line with Guess et al. (2019), we define fake news as 'false or misleading content intentionally dressed up to look like news articles'"
estimates.n: Daily total of georeferenced Indian tweets (not stated for 1 April 2020); 1,863,349 tweets in the two-week analysis window
estimates.source_quote: In line with the literature on the scapegoating of minorities during epidemic outbreaks (Jedwab et al., 2019), we document a large spike in anti-Muslim fake news on March 31: the share of tweets reporting anti-Muslim false stories – around 0.1% of total tweets in the week preceding the Tablighi shock – jumped to 2.8% on March 31, then peaked at 3.3% a day later.
estimates.page_loc: p. 2, Introduction (also Fig. 2 and p. 6: 'The share of anti-Muslim fake news peaked above 3% of total tweets on April 1')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Automated keyword/hashtag dictionary matching. The keyword list was seeded from the anti-Muslim false stories fact-checked by AltNews (a leading Indian fact-checking website) in March and April 2020, expanded by a snowball procedure and translated into 11 Indian languages (Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Gujarati, Marathi, Punjabi, Odia, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu, Bengali). Validation was indirect: Latent Dirichlet Allocation with five topics on the English-language matched tweets, of which topics 1, 3 and 5 were judged 'most likely to contain anti-Muslim false stories'. No per-tweet human verification of falsity, no precision/recall figures and no inter-coder reliability are reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: We obtained all georeferenced tweets published in India from December 1, 2019, to April 30, 2020 (Twitter API for academic research). This set of queries, conducted at the beginning of 2022, returned 16,967,380 tweets. [...] In our main exercise, we use the subset of tweets posted from March 24 to April 6, i.e., from one week before to one week after the Tablighi shock on March 30. This sample comprises 1,863,349 tweets published by 187,787 distinct users in 21,977 locations.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL for the adjudicator: this is a time series and the instructions require collapsing it to one representative point. I chose the stated PEAK (3.3% on 1 April 2020) because it is the paper's headline maximum and is stated verbatim. The two defensible alternatives, both verbatim in the same sentence, are 2.8% on 31 March 2020 (the shock day) and 'around 0.1% of total tweets in the week preceding the Tablighi shock' (the pre-shock baseline, which is an approximation, and which the paper elsewhere calls 'virtually zero'). A prevalence review may prefer the pre-shock baseline or a window average, since a single peak day overstates typical prevalence; no window average is reported. The daily denominator for 1 April is not stated, so the count behind 3.3% cannot be recovered. The measurement is keyword presence, not verified falsity of each tweet, so the numerator is broader than the fact-checked stories it was seeded from: the second keyword set ('Islamic Jihadis', 'Corona Jihadis') captures anti-Muslim rhetoric that is discriminatory but not necessarily a false factual claim. denom_scope=all_media because the denominator is every georeferenced tweet posted in India, not a topical corpus.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The pre-shock baseline 'around 0.1% of total tweets' and the 31 March value of 2.8% are alternative points on the same series and were not made into separate rows (the instruction is one representative point per time series); see the notes field. (2) Absolute hashtag counts (#Nizamuddin from 10,200 to over 114,000 tweets; #TablighiJamaat about 51,100; #NizamuddinIdiots 53,900; #TablighiJamatVirus 27,500) are counts from a third-party trends site (getdaytrends.com), with no denominator, so they fail R1/R8. (3) The daily district average of 3.38 fake-news tweets in the week after the shock is a per-district count, not a share, and its companion DID coefficients (-1.95, -1.38, +1.09 tweets, +1 tweet for historical Muslim attacks) are causal estimates, not prevalence. (4) 'almost 40% of the hate speech and disinformation fell under the category of Islamophobia' (footnote 7) is cited from Equity Labs/Soundararajan et al., is a share of hate-speech posts rather than of all content, and is a figure the paper cites from elsewhere: excluded by R8. (5) '57% of the respondents were concerned whether the online news they came across was real or fake' (footnote 6, Reuters Institute India 2019) is a concern measure cited from elsewhere, not an exposure or recall share, and is excluded on both grounds. (6) 'one in five Muslims say they have recently faced religious discrimination' and 'around 30% ... not willing to have Muslim neighbors' are attitude/discrimination measures cited from Pew and the World Values Survey, not misinformation exposure. (7) The language composition of the working dataset (40% English, 30% Hindi, 14% other, 16% unidentified) describes the corpus, not misinformation.

rob.design: Full census of georeferenced tweets published in India 1 December 2019 - 30 April 2020 obtained through the Twitter academic API in early 2022 (16,967,380 tweets); analysis restricted to tweets with a sub-state place identifier (about 84% of the pull), and the main window is 24 March - 6 April 2020 (1,863,349 tweets, 187,787 users, 21,977 locations), aggregated to 626 districts by day. Misinformation identified purely by a multilingual keyword/hashtag dictionary seeded from AltNews fact-checks and expanded by snowballing; validation is an unsupervised LDA topic model on the English matched subset, with no human verification of individual tweets, no precision/recall and no reliability statistics. Selection into the sample requires geolocation, which is a small and non-random slice of Indian Twitter, and Twitter itself is a non-representative slice of the Indian public; district-level Twitter penetration is controlled for in the regressions but not in the descriptive share. Standard errors clustered for spatial (250 km, Conley) and serial correlation.
rob.item6_quote: In line with Guess et al. (2019), we define fake news as "false or misleading content intentionally dressed up to look like news articles".
rob.item10_quote: Fig. 2 reports the share of tweets containing anti-Muslim fake news over the total number of tweets posted in a given day. [...] The share of anti-Muslim fake news peaked above 3% of total tweets on April 1, then steadily declined—though it remained above its preshock level one month later.
